dossier.public_summary: The dip sits on the K-dwarf star but its depth vanishes and reappears between TESS sectors and it has a second, deep eclipse and strong brightness swings at the same period. Its period matches the star's 4.6-day rotation signal. Together this is a stellar binary masquerading as a transit, not a planet.

reasons.why: Depth is not steady on target: AP flags changes_within_a_source (p_constant_all 7.893431954900835e-162). Per-sector depths range from -26 ppm in sector 37 to 1226 ppm in sector 10 (expected 472.5 ppm) – a 280.1% change that cannot be explained by a planet transit.

Significant second dip at 0.432 phase is ~26% as deep as the primary and above best_brightening_snr 10.83, plus large out-of-eclipse modulation ~47% of dip depth. Together this is stellar-binary signature, not a planet.
reasons.value: secondary snr 8.613 depth 121.4 ppm depth_over_dip 0.2605 phase 0.432; phase_curve amplitude 223.8 ppm ratio_to_depth 0.4737 chi2 546.4 dof 9

reasons.why: Signal period is essentially the measured stellar rotation period (96928 ppm amplitude) and shows large phase-curve chi2. Grazing V-shaped eclipse, long duration for the K-dwarf (1.55x central) and strong density penalty indicate the signal is on the target but is a spotted/rotating eclipsing binary, not a planet.
